analysis.title: Global Economics Outlook / US Equities / China Inflation / RBA's Hunter / APAC Tech
key_insights: UBS 2027-28 outlook: the AI infrastructure build-out has neutralized tariff and energy headwinds and drives over half of global trade growth, a large share of global GDP growth, and half of year-to-date equity gains. The outlook depends on the build-out continuing and on some resolution in the Middle East, the main source of growth acceleration in 2027.

Bottom-up aggregation points to $1.75 trn of hyperscaler capex next year, but public opposition to data centres could delay and reprofile near-term spending. Enterprise adoption remains low and AI implementation spending is unusually concentrated.

Economist Arend Kapetyn expects a progressively more disinflationary 2027 as inflation from tariffs, energy and memory price fades. He expects only modest additional tightening, then a reversal of the hikes in 2028. Global equity earnings growth is running at the 91st historical percentile.

UBS cross-asset positioning: favour Nasdaq over RTY, industrials over consumer, growth over value. Favour steepeners in the US and flatteners in Europe, as terminal rates look mispriced across most markets. Favour long gold vs EUR and long JPY vs CHF.

Hedge fund derivatives sales (Michael Romano) expects US equities to stay vulnerable early this week with another test of the 200-day moving average likely. Squeeze risk is acute, and if the clearing event comes without deterioration in credit, rates or FX, the desk would add risk rather than protection.

None of the circuit breakers discussed as catalysts to fresh highs have manifested over the past 2 months. Rate pressure turned into funding pressure, oil rose as the Mideast conflict continued, hyperscaler earnings fell short and Democrats dominated the mid-terms. Investors have demanded a large discount to hold AI risk and moved money from Tech into credit.
Systematic selling triggered over 365bn of excess sell flow on Thursday, the largest on record. Most systematic selling is behind the market, but the larger issue is the absence of long-only demand.

Structuring strategist Rebecca Cheong expects one more pocket of forced selling into Monday, with possible multi-strategy deleveraging starting in Asia hours plus $85-115bn of risk control selling. She expects a sharp recovery afterward given the Nov. 5 capitulation signals, strong real money support and very low hedge fund and systematic positioning.

Positioning is light: UBS PB L/S, CTA and RC exposures sit at 4%, 5% and 0%-tile vs 1Y, while stock short interest is above the 90th percentile vs 5Y. Target Date Funds saw +$29 bn of November inflows so far, foreign-listed US ETF buying reached +2.4x STD, and UBS RMM bought 4 of 4 dip days over the past two weeks.
Corporate buybacks have one more low-seasonality week before returning to $35-55 bn per week until early January.

This week's FOMC speakers include Governor Waller, Vice Chair Bowman and Philadelphia Fed President Paulson (a voting member). Economist Jonathan Pingle expects a 0.25pp hike in December, another in January, then a pause. CPI is Tuesday and PPI is Friday, and the desk cautions against over-reading PCE translations between the two.

The next two catalysts are US CPI on Tuesday and Nvidia earnings on Nov. 17. Economist Alan Detmeister expects October core CPI +0.23% and headline +0.26%, helped by gasoline and used vehicles. Both events imply roughly a 1% SPX move, among the largest event-implied moves left through year-end.

China October CPI rose 0.7% y/y, below September's 0.9% and the 0.8% consensus. PPI rose 5.7% y/y vs 5.0% prior and 5.3% expected, the highest since June 2022, driven by higher oil prices. Weak household demand held back consumer inflation, which could complicate efforts to revive consumption while supporting industry.

RBA Chief Economist Sarah Hunter said there is limited evidence that AI has materially lifted aggregate productivity and sees some upward pressure on inflation. Higher investment demand could raise the neutral rate. Economist George Tharenou expects the RBA to keep the cash rate restrictive for a prolonged time.

BoE Chief Economist Huw Pill said rates could stay on hold or even fall if growth stalls. He called the last hike preemptive and said the UK should not see a repeat of 2022's aggressive hikes. SONIA futures ended slightly lower Friday and gilts underperformed, with 10y yields up 2bp on the week.

EURUSD screens cheap at -0.8σ. FX Strategy is bearish EUR at 1.105 for FY26 and 1.10 for FY27, but expects spot to recover toward 1.13 as the widening OATs-Bunds spread that drove EURUSD from 1.15 to 1.11 in about thirty trading days fades.

China's State Council extended the suspension of the 24% additional tariff on US imports for two months from Tuesday and retains a 10% tariff. This followed Beijing's objection to new US sanctions on two Chinese companies during a call between Vice Premier He Lifeng, Treasury Secretary Bessent and USTR Greer.

APAC Tech is down 39% quarter to date and 58% from the June peak, with valuations at 14.7x 28E PE vs 23.7x before. Samsung and SK Hynix trade at 0.79x and 0.98x 28E P/B. UBS Research prefers memory, semicap and MLCCs, is Overweight Korea tech, upgrades Japan to Overweight, cuts Taiwan to Neutral and stays Underweight China.

Hyperscaler and neocloud capex is forecast at $1.77 trn in 2027 (+70% y/y) against $1.45 trn of operating cash flow, leaving about $312 bn of negative free cash flow. Memory could consume $1.02 trn, or 58% of capex.

China equity strategist James Wang recommends banks, telecoms and utilities, plus under-owned property and consumer stocks with shareholder returns above 5%, screened for high free cash flow and low short interest. A-shares may be less defensive now because of higher tech hardware exposure.

APAC flows: Korea, Japan and Taiwan had a double-digit AI-led selloff. Korean foreign selling overwhelmed local buyers, Japanese hedge funds sold semiconductor equipment while long-only accounts bought defensives. India and China were countercurrents, with China internet and tech ETF buying and India banks and autos leading.

Japan equities surged in morning trade: Nikkei +3.4%, TOPIX +0.43%, with 1,602 of 1,668 TOPIX stocks advancing. Flows were 55% better to buy, with the desk buying retail and MLCCs and selling semiconductor production equipment.

Friday's US session was a narrow chip-led rebound: S&P 500 +31bp, Nasdaq 100 +135bp, but only 44% of S&P names advanced and the median stock fell 0.24%. The Stoxx 600 fell 100bp. The US 10-year yield rose 2.27bp to 4.86% after a hot October jobs report, with around 20bp of tightening priced for December, and Brent traded near $98.
